utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters, the registry staff, the counsel for the Prosecution and the counsel for the Defence. Here we are to continue our proceedings with the testimony, which we started yesterday. Yes, Mr. Jovan Simic. You have some news for us? Bad news? MR. J. SIMIC: Good morning, Your Honours. Unfortunately, we do have bad news. Mr. Prcac is not well again. He was transferred yesterday from the Tribunal two or three hours later. He didn't have a good night and he couldn't come today. He has written a memo. I don't know exactly what it is. I spoke to him this morning. He's not well at all. As usual, we suggest we continue in his absence and hope that he will be back with us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, when you said that he was transferred two or three hours later, what did you mean? Has the question we discussed before been resolved? What is the situation, please? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, last time when President Jorda was -- visited the Detention Unit, as well as Mr. McFadden, an agreement was reached that conditions would change and that Mr. Prcac would be transferred differently, that he would get a lighter vest because this one is very heavy for him. That started functioning. However, there was a problem with medicines. And as soon as we have a recess, things seem to be forgotten, and the decision is not observed of Mr. McFadden and President Jorda. It is no longer a problem with the other accused because the Prosecution has rescinded that request that they be transported separately. They can come together. I don't really know why this problem is occurring. Our case is approaching, and we simply cannot count on Mr. Prcac's presence. This decision is there. Why it is not being fully implemented, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please take note of this and convey this part of the transcript to the President of the Tribunal so that the necessary measures be taken to implement his decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us resume our case. Mr. Usher, can you have the witness brought in, please? Being a protected witness, we have to lower the blinds for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness DD/5. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind you that you are still testifying under oath, and you will still be answering questions from the Prosecution. Ms. Susan Somers, please, your witness to finish the cross-examination

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Somers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DD/5, referring back to Prosecution's Exhibit 3/251 from yesterday, which is a statement you indicated that you signed but under duress, I would like to ask you pursuant to your comment about this statement which is on page 10026 of the official transcript, you said, "I did sign it, but I didn't say everything that is stated here in this statement." I would like to ask you what, in fact, you did state that is in the statement, or perhaps if you could tell me, rapidly as we are under time pressure, whether or not the following points in the statement were given under coercion. Were you coerced into telling the persons taking this statement that you left Keraterm camp for Omarska camp after nine days in Keraterm? Were you coerced into saying that you left after nine days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Omarska on the 13th day, and what I said over there, I said all that under coercion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to confirm your arrival date in Keraterm, you put that as the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're telling us that the nine days in Keraterm from the 30th, which would put you at approximately the 7th or 8th of June leaving for Omarska, that that was coerced; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I went from Keraterm to the Omarska camp on the 13th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it also coerced when in the statement it indicated that at Omarska, and this is page 2 of the English, "The camp warden was Zeljko Meakic, a policeman from Prijedor, who was around 30 years old. His deputy was," you give a first name of "Zoran," but last name, "Kvocka who was also a policeman before the war. They were around 5.000 inmates, mostly Bosniaks." Were those also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a very brief objection. The witness said that he was forced to sign this statement. Never has he said nor explained whether he's familiar with the contents of this statement. The Prosecution, ever since they started the cross-examination until the present moment, are proceeding as if he's familiar with the contents of the statement, and all of us sitting here don't know whether that is so or not. So my objection is that after the witness said that he did sign the statement, was he familiar with the contents of that statement. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, I understood that Ms. Susan Somers referred to the transcript when the witness said that there were statements that he made under coercion and others not. Now Ms. Susan Somers is trying to see whether this statement on paper was signed under duress or not, and the witness has the opportunity to say whether he signed this particular part of the statement under coercion or not, once the witness makes a distinction between those statements that he signed under coercion and others that he did not sign under coercion. So it is quite legitimate to make this distinction now, Mr. Deretic. In any event, I'm going to give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers to respond to this objection and to confirm whether I understood her correctly or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You understood me absolutely correctly, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, your objection is overruled, and please do not make these objections. We have a framework. I'm asking the Prosecutor to respect those frameworks and guidelines, and also I'm asking you to respect them. Otherwise, we will not be able to proceed in this way. Is that clear now, Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make things quite clear, however, Ms. Susan Somers, you may repeat the page of the transcript where the witness made this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was the official page 10026, ten thousand zero two six, and it would be lines 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Deretic, you can say whether the witness said that or not, and after that, you must allow the Prosecutor to do her work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not wish anything to remain vague. I'm not quite sure that you understood my objection. May I say just one sentence? My objection is that until this moment, we still do not know whether after signing this statement the witness was familiarised with the content of that statement. That was my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you are making that objection in very general terms, because the Prosecutor is reading to the witness and saying, "In this statement of which you said that a part was signed and coercion and another part was not, so I'm asking, 'Is this particular part, under coercion or not?'" So he does know the content. You're making a general observation. But if we look at what is being done now, then your objection doesn't stand at all, Mr. Deretic. We have to use our common sense. You understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the witness is not familiar with the content and therefore he cannot be asked about the content. Yes. Okay. But that is precisely why Ms. Susan Somers is reading a part of the statement to ask him, "Did you say this under force or not?" That's all. Ms. Susan Somers, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony yesterday mentioned a fair amount about Becir Medunjanin, who died in the Omarska camp. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before this discussion was opened, Ms. Somers read out certain parts of an alleged statement and they have become a part of the record. However, we haven't heard the reply, whether the witness did make that part of the statement under coercion or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Susan Somers, I think if you asked the question, we have to get the answer. So perhaps you could go back a little and repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. The question did have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dusan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The interruption, I think, just threw us off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question which was part of my original question was: Was the sentence about the camp warden, being Zeljko Meakic, a policeman from Prijedor, who was around 30 years old, and his deputy was, you list first name Zoran, last name Kvocka, who was also a policeman before the war and that there were around 5.000 inmates, mostly Bosniaks and some Croats in the camp, were those items also made under coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the question about Becir Medunjanin, who died in Omarska camp, which you acknowledged, the lack of any mention in the statement which you indicated you believe to have been made under coercion is puzzling given yesterday's emphasis that you placed on your knowledge about his beatings and his death. You yourself indicated that, and I quote: "That Medunjanin was a main organiser of the attack on Prijedor from Kozarac." You were in the hands of the Bosnian officials. Medunjanin was a senior official of the Bosniak side. Were you asked any questions, if you recollect, about Medunjanin to be answered in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me any questions about Medunjanin, but when I arrived at the Omarska camp, I asked the detainees, the prisoners, when I saw the condition he was in, bloodied, lying down, who the man was. I hadn't known him before the war or during the war, until I reached the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement which you indicated that you believed to have been made under coercion, there is a sentence which reads: "I wish to stress that when the investigators completed their questionings, they left a list of people who were to be liquidated that night and they would give the list to the guards. That evening, the names of the men would be called out and they would be taken away and killed." Was that statement which described the relationship between the interrogators and the guards done under coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when the Omarska camp was dismantled when we went to Manjaca and to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not clear that your answer responded to my question. Was that statement made under coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about your recollection of an incident where Duca, Dusan Knezevic, made a threat to a person you described as being Emsud Bahonjic. Do you recall talking about Duca holding a knife to someone's throat who allegedly confessed to killing his brother? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having had a night to think about your testimony, have you concluded, perhaps, or possibly that you may have gotten that wrong, that in fact it was Fajzo Mujkanovic whose throat was cut by Duca, not the person named Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujkanovic came from Kozarac. When he arrived already, he had a cut throat, and the wounds were already healing. There was a scab forming on his neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard testimony about an incident where Duca put a knife to the throat of Mujkanovic and brought his family in, threatening to kill them if Mujkanovic didn't tell him about the death of his brother. Are you suggesting that perhaps that testimony is confused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how many other people, and their names, were transported with you from Keraterm to Omarska. I'd like some of the names of those detainees, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the names because they were people from Raskovac and Cejreci that were transferred with me to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We talked about a person yesterday named Tokmadzic. You discussed your perceptions or observations of various aspects of his time in Keraterm. You were gone from Keraterm when he arrived as a detainee, weren't you? You only saw him when he was bringing in detainees because he himself was a policeman who, to some degree, cooperated with the Serbs. You never saw him as a detainee, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him for about two days in the Keraterm camp, Drago Tokmadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the physical layout of Keraterm camp, and again, perhaps having had the night to think about what you said yesterday, have you thought about the location of Rooms 1 and 2? They were adjoining rooms, were they not? Room 1 was adjoining to Room 2. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday when you indicated a separation, that was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was about two or three metres between the doors of the two rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin, returning to Omarska for a moment, was already in Omarska when you arrived, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no idea of the history of the beatings that were dealt to Becir Medunjanin before your arrival, do you? You have no idea.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know if Zoran Zigic, the accused, on whose behalf you're here to testify, may have given him some of those beatings before you arrived, do you? You have no idea of what happened before your arrival; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before my arrival, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm trying to wind down. I just want to see if there's any other questions. Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Deretic for any re-examination, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DD/5, can you briefly, in a single sentence, explain what your work obligation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To dig trenches and dugouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradacac, Olovo, and Zuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the digging of these trenches between the front lines of the VRS and the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was some 20 to 30 metres away, depending on where we were digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you directly exposed to the fire of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, like a human shield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of your comrades were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Six [as interpreted] of the men digging with me were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you again repeat the number how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 600 were killed by the BH army in the labour platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement you gave on the 11th of October, 1994, or actually, which is attributed to you, was it given while you were in Travnik or in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you put your signature on the statement, was it read out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the content of that statement when you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did -- I was not familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were signing that statement, were you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DD/5, you were shown yesterday an order for the issuance of a wanted warrant. Did you know anything at all about that order until yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only a few days ago I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone call you up from the Public Security Centre in Prijedor before Friday for any kind of interview to tell you that there was any kind of order or a wanted warrant issued against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you visited the international police force in Prijedor a few days ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the gentleman from the international police force tell you anything about the existence of such an order or a wanted warrant for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a wanted warrant has been issued against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you did sell some cigarettes in the compound on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute please. You said that you sold cigarettes on one occasion. Did you sell those on behalf of Zigic, Zoran?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on behalf of soldiers. I said yesterday, I sold two or three packets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you heard that Ms. Somers mentioned Fajzo Mujkanovic as a person whose neck was slit. Is he alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is alive. Fajzo Mujkanovic is in a third country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen him since the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen him, but I have heard from the Kozarusa people, from where my late father is, that Fajzo is in a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DD/5, you said that you spent, I think, four days, three or four days in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic in the "white house" during those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DD/5. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a few questions to ask you. You mentioned -- I'll just start with the beginning of your testimony. When you spoke about Mr. Zigic, you said that he would not do anybody any harm but you would hear him shouting to the soldiers. Was that a sign of his importance that he would order the soldiers around in the camp, and would they fear him and obey him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Zigic was shouting, he was having pains in his left hand all the time, the left hand that was bandaged, and so he was suffering a great deal and had a lot of pain. So he shouted at us detainees and at the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, was he shouting because he was in pain, was he drunk, or was he in authority, had the authority to shout, to give orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just because his hand hurt him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he was going around shouting out of pain, that's all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Zigic never called anybody out for beating. You knew his voice, that's the reason, but how could you tell who was beating people outside? The people beating were not seen, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the door to our room was open all day, up until 9.00 or 10.00 at night. And Zoran Zigic, I personally didn't see him beat or mistreat anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that you are testifying for Mr. Zigic because he was good to you and to your brothers in the camp. Was this a special treatment and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was treated like all the other detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, the other detainees did not come to testify for him. You said that he was good to you and to your brothers. Was he good to everybody, of the same level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. I think that how he behaved towards us was how he behaved to the rest of the inmates as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that you wouldn't go back to anyplace in the Mostar area because you used the word -- you said people would eat you up. Why would they feel like that towards you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me tell you this way: When I went to Muslim territory in 1994, I spent six years and three months in a camp there with the Muslims, under the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why? Were they putting Muslims in prison, in camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant prison. When I said "camp," I meant prison. And I spent six years and three months in prison. And in the Republika Srpska, I passed through three camps and never saw the suffering that I saw take place in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean six years and a half in prison for being accused of killing Fajzo Mujkanovic or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because of Mujkanovic. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you discovered later that Mujkanovic is alive in a third country. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you consider informing the authorities about that or making your own research to, let's say, clear your reputation, even if you didn't care to go back to the Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know about this Fajzo father's until several days ago, before I was supposed to leave here, when he came to visit my mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And after that you did not take any action. Do you intend to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke about -- you said that it was Duca who cut -- you said he cut the throat of, I think - what was the name? - of Emsud Bahonjic just in front of his family. Was that a recurrent event, just people cutting everybody's throat in public like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only once, that once when Emsud --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect for Judge Riad, I must say that a -- that he is asking questions starting out from an observation that Duca slit Emsud's throat, and nobody mentioned that to this day. Absolutely nobody made any mention of that, and I don't know where the Judge got this question from, and I must react, with all due respect for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, and with all respect too, I would give the floor to Judge Riad if he has an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And speaking of due respect, I have the greatest respect of Mr. Deretic, and I request that in the break we look at the transcript, because I noted down that mister -- that Emsud Bahonjic was beaten by Duca and by other soldiers, and he was accused of killing the brother, the brother of Duca, and that Duca cut his throat in front of his people. It is here. The witness is there and the transcript is here. And I would even go as far as asking to -- asking the President to adjourn to find out if this is noted down or not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I could suggest another method of procedure. I think that the witness is here in the courtroom and that he can answer your question, and we will hear the witness' answer. So please proceed, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, but I request from the registrar to bring us the transcript later. Would you like to answer this question, Witness DD/5? The question is: Did it happen that people be killed openly, in plain daylight like that in the camp in front of others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that was a very exceptional event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't even -- when mother, father, and child, they would just beat them. Fighting, they were fighting, and they would beat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who would be fighting, the -- who would be fighting, the soldiers with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and with Duca Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you mean that Emsud was fighting with Duca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Duca beat Emsud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. You said he brought his family, and he finished by cutting his throat, just for my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't cut his throat, but he did bring his family in and returned his family to the Trnopolje camp, to the collection centre there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he did not cut his throat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We'll have to verify the transcript. You said that you were digging trenches. You went with the army of Republika Srpska to dig trenches, and you were mobilised to work with a platoon. Were you -- did you volunteer, or were you chosen to do that, taken by force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We received the order from the civilian authorities in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you about the statement 3/251, 3/251. You said you made it under duress, so I won't ask you about the content except, perhaps, your opinion about something they asked you. As you said, they told you to do -- to say what they wanted. They asked you to say that Duca would beat the inmate, and you -- you yourself said that Duca was doing that. And then they asked you to say also that Zoran Zigic did that. Why did they choose Zigic in particular, in your opinion, to tell you to speak about him? What did they -- did they consider him also -- I mean, there were so many people. Why did they tell you to speak about Zigic, in your opinion? What did they have against him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't understand your question. I don't know what you mean, what did they have against him. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, did they chose him because he's an important person? They didn't, they didn't mention ten people here; they mentioned only two, Duca and Zigic. And Duca in fact was, as you said, committed, so why did they add Zigic from all other people, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. The statement I made in Travnik, I said what I said because I was beaten and said everything that didn't happen because they thought that I was a Muslim traitor while I was there until the 17th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Mr. Deretic, there was a question that was raised by you, and I should like to straighten things out to have the matter clear. I will give you the opportunity of saying whether, after the questions by the Judges and Judge Riad's question, whether you wish to pose additional questions to the witness, and I'm going to ask the Prosecutor the same thing afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just have one question. When you spoke yesterday -- you mean to go ahead and ask the witness now? I didn't quite understand you, Your Honour. Do you mean now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but only following the questions from Judge Riad, based on the questions asked by Judge Riad, the question that troubled you. So we're not going to reopen the examination and cross-examination. You indicated that there was a point that was not clear, so only within that framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Mr. President. Further re-examination by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when you spoke about Emsud Bahonjic and when you said -- when you talked about a person that had his throat slit and you mentioned Duca Knezevic, did you mean Emsud Bahonjic or did you mean Igor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Igor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is where the problem lay, Mr. President. So it was Duca's brother whose throat was slit when the question arose concerning Emsud Bahonjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. This isn't the moment to make any other allegations. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would, of course, have to object that counsel effectively signalled the response, and we would ask the Court to give it the way that it should be attributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I think we all should. I did not ask you to interpret the witness's answer, that is where the problem lay. We just wanted to hear the witness's answer and not your interpretation of it. But having said that, I'll now give the floor to Judge Wald. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness DD/5, I have a few relatively straightforward questions to ask you. One, I believe you testified here that during the process of being interrogated at Omarska, you were beaten; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Who beat you? Was it specifically the interrogators themselves or soldiers or guards at the camp, at Omarska, that beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know from your personal knowledge whether or not the interrogators told the soldiers to beat you or the soldiers beat you on their own whim or will? Could you tell that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the orders came from the inspectors, the inspectors that interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you saw or heard the inspectors tell the soldiers to beat you? I'm just trying to get that straight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in Keraterm you told us about observations you had about Duca beating people, and I believe in Omarska, too. Duca, now. Did you ever see in Keraterm Zigic and Duca together? You told us you never saw Zigic in Omarska, but you did see him on occasion in Keraterm. Did you ever see Zigic and Duca together? I'm not saying a beating was going on or anything. Did you just ever see them together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, perhaps I did see them once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: At Keraterm;, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that you, for a period, were out in Omarska, were out on the pista, and that you spent every night during that period on the pista; is that right? During the period that you were on the pista at Omarska, that you spent every night there during the period you were there. Not the period you were in the "white house," but in the period that you were in the pista. That you spent nights on the pista; is that correct? I have that in my notes, but tell me if they're not correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there all the time when I left the "white house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent all my time on the pista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. In other words, you spent both nights and days. That's all I'm trying to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, vis-a-vis this disputed warrant for the arrest or order for the arrest, document 3/252, which you told us you did not know about until a few days ago, my question to you is, after you returned -- after you didn't return from the weekend leave, you told us about that yesterday. You just didn't go back after the third weekend leave. Now, to your knowledge then, back then, which would have been back in 2000, I think, in the spring, March or April of 2000, if I have it correct, at that time was there any communication that you heard about by letter, by telephone call, either to you or to your relatives asking where you were and why you weren't coming back? Did you ever hear about anybody at that time making inquiries about why you didn't come back, where you were, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean why I didn't go back to prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Just, did you ever hear, when you didn't go back to prison, did you ever get a letter? Did you ever have one of your relatives say they were asking about you, they were calling about you? Did you in any way know that they had tried to make contact with you when you didn't return, back then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, on the back of the 3/252 which you were given, it says on the -- that the convict may be located in, and it gives an address, Bugojno, number 49 Crnicka Street where it says you were domiciled. Did you in fact return to that address, or did you, once you didn't return to prison, live at a different address than that which is on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Bugojno. It was Crnicka 49, Crnicka Street number 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So, good. I mean "good" that I'm understanding better. When you did not return to prison after the third weekend, you did go back to the same address which is on this document, namely, 49 Crnicka Street, Bugojno, right? That's where you just stayed. You just stayed there. You didn't return to prison and you just stayed at that address, at least for a while; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed there. On the third day when I left Bugojno, when I left the house from Bugojno and went back to prison -- I went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, you didn't go back to prison, you went someplace else. Okay. But to your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Prijedor, yes. I didn't go back, I went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Did any of your relatives continue to live at that address, or was there anybody there that you knew that continued to stay at that address, or any relative or not, after you left to go back to Prijedor. After you left to go back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my late father and my mother came a few days before I fled. They came to Prijedor. And while I was in Bugojno, I had a sort of presentiment that my father would die. And my wife and children stayed on in Bugojno but now they're in Prijedor too. They came to Prijedor last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. And just to finish up this question, your wife and children stayed on a little while, but to your knowledge, nobody contacted them about why you didn't go back to prison after the weekend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, in the cantonal or military court which sentenced you to the seven years in prison in the Federation, do you know who testified against you in that proceeding? You don't have to give me names, but just was it other detainees in Omarska or was there live witnesses - you don't have to give their names - were there live witnesses who testified against you in the proceeding which led to your prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All those who accused me were those who were with me in the Omarska camp, and when I went to the Federation in 1994, I received an accusation from those people who accused me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, you were present at that trial; is that correct? I mean you were there while the trial was going on that led to your prison sentence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us just an approximation of the number of witnesses from -- not their names, just an approximation of the number of witnesses from the camp that testified against you in that proceeding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were about 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my last couple of questions deal with the disputed statement. I wanted to get it clear. When the statement that you say was signed under coercion was made, were you, in fact, asked any questions and gave any answers even under coercion or did somebody simply present you with a full-fledged statement, not show you or tell you what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 was in it, and say, "Sign it"? Which of the -- it could be -- even if it was under coercion, it could be one of either. It could be either that you felt you were under coercion and they asked you questions and told you what answers they wanted you to give them, or it could be they just presented you with a statement and said, "Sign it or else," sort of thing. Which of those happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, madam, when I went to that military court, I only said a few sentences to that gentleman there, but when I was deported to Zenica, eight months later when I received the indictment, there were 200 pages of it written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's make sure we're talking about the same thing here. You said that you signed the statement under coercion in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, that would have been before, am I right? Would have been before, or would it have been after the trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Before the trial. Okay. Now, before the trial when you signed the statement - I'm just trying to understand - did they give you the statement and say, "Sign it here or," whatever, "you'll be beaten up," or did you have an interview with them in which they asked you questions and then wrote whatever statement they wanted to, or did they say, "Here's the question and here's the answer we want you to give"? Did they interview you at all, even under coercion, or did they just hand you the statement and say, "Sign it"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there on the 17th of September, 1994, 29 days in military detention, and throughout that time, that whole time, they beat us in Travnik. They beat me. And they just brought a piece of paper, statement, and just said, "Sign this." And they said, "When you sign it, you can read it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So is that what happened, that you signed it and then they let you read it? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you did read it at that time, after you signed it under coercion, according to your statement. You read it then. Did you say anything to them after you read it? I know you had already signed it and according to your testimony the signing was under coercion, but after you read it, as you just told us that you did read it, did you then say anything to them about, "None of that is true," or, "You've got it all wrong," or did you not say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that, madam, but there was nobody to tell that to because we were criminals for them according to the statements that they had rigged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and this is my last question, but I just want to make sure I have it correct. What you're telling us now is that this five -- whatever, four- or five-page statement here, that somebody else wrote it from beginning to end before they talked to you and just gave it to you to sign, all of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And had they -- had those same authorities ever, before they gave it to you, not that day but before that, talked to you about what happened in the camp, or they just made it up out of their minds without even talking to you once? Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody talked to us in the 29 days we were there. Not a single word did they exchange with us. All they did was beat us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness DD/5, I also have a few questions for you, and the first is this: What was the very first time in your life that you met Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Zoran Zigic for the first time in my life seven or eight years perhaps prior to the war. That is how long I have known him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under which circumstances did you meet him seven or eight years prior to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, while Zoran Zigic was a taxi driver at the railway station and the bus-stop, I knew a number of other taxi drivers as well. There was somebody called Omer and Meho, and we would talk and that's how I met him. I knew him as a taxi driver, as a man, as a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you arrived at Keraterm, was it easy for you to recognise Zoran Zigic because you knew him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already know, and you told Judge Wald that you did see Zigic with Duca once at Keraterm. How many times did you see Zoran Zigic in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 30th of May until the 13th of June, 1992, I saw Zoran about ten times in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten times? Which would mean almost every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every day, but he would come two or three times during the day. He would come and go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I should also like to come back to the question of your statement. Do you remember the date when, according to you, you were forced to sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The statement in Travnik, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I signed it roundabout the 25th of October or the 26th. Something like that. Just before I had to appear before the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understood that you mentioned declarations in the plural. How many statements have you signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I signed two statements, but they were quite big, lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say they were rather long, what do you mean by "long"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They consisted of about ten pages to one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other one? How many pages did that one have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count, but more or less the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you signed the declarations. How many signatures did you give, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the usher to put before the witness Exhibit 3/253. I think he has that exhibit. It's the statement. What is the problem? 251, I think, Judge Wald reminds me. It's Exhibit 251. Witness, you have the statement in front of you in your own language? Could the usher assist the witness, please. I want to check that the witness does have the exhibit in front of him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Tell me, how many pages did you sign here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I count them now, because I really don't remember? It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remember signing this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you recognise your signature? Is that indeed your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 4, there's another signature. Do you know that person, the person who signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Oh, you mean this one, Zijad. Is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did this person sign the document at the same time as you or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, with respect to this statement -- you told Judge Wald, "I said what I said in Travnik because I was under coercion." What did you mean when you said, "I said what I said"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under coercion. You see, when I got to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Turbe when we changed buses, they separated the elderly, women, and children from the others and drove them off to Bugojno. As for us men, all able-bodied men were driven to the barracks. And after two hours there in the barracks, I was in civilian clothes and, as I said yesterday, a man came up to me. I don't know who he is or what he is. He cursed my mother, and I said, "Why are you cursing me?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've heard all that. But Witness DD/5, when you say, "I said what I said under coercion," did someone force you to say something and you said what they wrote down? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was forced and I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that. I think I can believe that you were coerced, but the question is, you were under coercion, but you said what you said under coercion, but did you say it under coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So somebody drafted the document beforehand and forced you to sign it. That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all done under beatings. They were beating me, my brother, and a neighbour of mine, because, sir, we were beaten up day and night there for 29 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that. But finally, Witness DD/5, what you signed here, you signed it, and you actually said that under coercion and you signed it under coercion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question. How is your family living? What are the means of livelihood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have nothing. I earn a bit. I earn something here. I go here and there to earn five, ten marks, to do something, to do odd jobs. And that is how we live, my wife and my five children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness DD/5, we have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that perhaps before the break, there are two -- or one small question that I should like to address with Mr. Jovan Simic. I have been informed, though I haven't yet received a motion, I think that you requested a videolink for a witness, Mr. Jovan Simic. Can you briefly answer this question: Is this a new witness, an additional witness? Secondly, what are the reasons for a videolink with him? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to say first that all our witnesses are actually new. We did give you a list, and as far as I remember, you gave us permission to amend that list because we joined the case late. In the course of these proceedings certain things have emerged, and the Defence of Mr. Prcac has identified those things and has decided to call 14 or 15 witnesses. One of those is the one for whom we have suggested a videolink. He is a Serb who worked in the Omarska Investigation Centre for a time, not in the centre itself but in the Separacija, and who was later captured. He spent 274 days in detention. He was the last Serb to be exchanged before the truce was signed over there, who suffered a great deal, who gave a statement listing names regarding the organisation and functioning of the Omarska Investigation Centre or camp. This is a statement that was used by the Prosecution, and we wanted to call him. He has suffered a lot. Psychologically, he is not in a condition to travel. He is an only child. His parents are very old, and he takes care of them. And believe me, when we appeared it was a great shock for them. Any unknown person who appears provokes fear in them that he will never come back. We have taken an affidavit from him, but we hope the Chamber would allow us to have a videolink because we think live contact would be far more convincing and reliable, and it is always better for the Chamber to see a person, even by means of video, than simply to have an affidavit or a deposition from a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I don't know whether you have received -- have the privilege of receiving the motion. Is there anything you wish to say? Because we need to decide as soon as possible so as to be able to organise the week for the videolink. Ms. Susan Somers, do you have any opinion about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received the motion late yesterday. The witness, in fact, was mentioned. A statement, although unsigned, was mentioned during the cross-examination of one of the witnesses, I believe in the Kvocka part of the evidence. My information on this witness differs considerably from that which Mr. Simic has. My understanding is he is an official in the RS government in a major section of the government. I am not convinced that there is any reason why he could not travel here, and I would ask, I would ask that there be provided medical evidence of inability to travel. I can see no reason not to have this individual live here. Additionally, it will be taken out of order because none of the Prcac evidence will have been given, and I do not know that there will not be more videolinks, but the request is that he would testify during -- at the tail-end of the evidence coming up next week which would greatly disadvantage, I think, the Prosecution in being able to question him. Therefore, on two grounds, one is that I'm not convinced on behalf of the Prosecution that this witness cannot come here based on information that we have received about him; and secondly, I think it will not allow us effectively to cross-examine him in the absence of putting the case to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I was waiting for the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and when there's overlapping, it's difficult to follow. I was waiting for the French interpretation. Please go ahead, Judge Wald, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure. If he were a live witness, you wouldn't have any say in what order he came in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If he were a live witness and came here, you wouldn't be able to control whether he was the first witness or the second witness or the third witness, right? I'm just trying to understand what your complaint is about the order in which he testifies since, you know, it's pretty much up to the Defence, would know this ahead of time as to what order they put their witnesses on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is part of the problem, Your Honour. We are not clear of the order of the witnesses for the Prcac case, and our arrangements of getting the information with which we will conduct cross-examination depends heavily on order. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you just want foreknowledge, but you can't control the order --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- in which they put on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Also, I would remind -- or at least, this is only my reaction, maybe not you, I can't remember, but the Prosecution has used videolink in cases that were not -- physical inability of witnesses to come, so what's sauce for the goose might be sauce for the gander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and I'm sure it was not during my time on this case. However, I will indicate that my understanding of the limitations is somewhat different, and perhaps if we could get some official clarification of reasons, it would make it easier for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make sure that I understand you, Ms. Susan Somers, the question of order, is that decisive for you, the order in which this witness appears?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is correct that we have no control whatsoever over order; however, it assists us certainly in trying to meet the case if we know what to ask. I think the interests of justice would merit that he -- that if we're going to go immediately into the Zigic case, that we could at least get an order of which witnesses will definitively testify. I've had some discussions with Mr. Jovan Simic, and it is unclear -- it is not likely, apparently, at this point in time that the accused will take the stand, from what I am told. So we are trying very hard to formulate our cross-examination, which, of course, is done -- I'm sorry, I said -- I want to correct the transcript. It should read into the Prcac case. I said Zigic case on line 10 of page 36. It would make the Prosecution's presentation of its cross-examination more effective to know where we are going, and inasmuch as time is very much a concern, rather than lose time, I think it would be helpful for us in, in fact, the Chamber is satisfied that medically this individual cannot come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, we have to move forward. There's only the following question: If Mr. Jovan Simic gives you a summary of the statement of the witness he wishes to examine by video conference at least five days in advance, are you capable of cross-examining him?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are, that's fine. Thank you, Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Jovan Simic, your response. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to respond to my learned friend. This is an individual who has had experiences similar to those of Prosecution witnesses, going through various camps in Bosnia. He simply is not ready to leave his family. It may sound naive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you, but that is not contested. The question raised by Ms. Susan Somers was that this was somebody linked to the government with great responsibilities. That is the point you have to respond to. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't quite understand. This is not a senior official of the government. It's an ordinary man from a village close to Omarska who is a waiter and who happened to have experienced what he did during the war. He is no president, deputy, or anything else in the government. I can give you his name, his name is Drasko Djervida. He is not prime minister or deputy or candidate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, a quick response because we have to finish with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Our information, Your Honour, having tried to get some background is that he works for the custom service of the RS, I think it was in Bosanska, perhaps Dubica, unless we've been given wrong information. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he is working as a guard but not as a customs officer. He is a watchman of a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the problem is that there are several people with the same name. Ms. Somers, we're told he's a watchman of a customs warehouse. Does that pose a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I suspect that it's because there's a concession that it was a customs-related job. No, I was not given the designation or rank but that he was employed by the RS customs service, gainfully employed, working person. And this is in response, Your Honour, to allegations of limitation, potential invalidity. Your Honour, it is possible that this individual will be called before the opening statement? Is this something the Court would agree to or is agreeing to? Because this would involve calling a witness prior to opening statement of the Prcac case. Does this have any impact on the Court's decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any difficulty there. As you know, the Chamber may modify the order of the presentation of evidence. The only problem, Ms. Susan Somers, is the following: Since all the equipment and personnel are in Banja Luka for the video-conference, then we would have to send for a single witness the whole setup. As you know, we've always tried to group video-conferences into one week. The fact that we haven't heard the opening statement, in my opinion, in my opinion, is no problem. But we would also like to hear the views of the parties. I don't see any problem there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think -- our position of course is that if the Chamber is satisfied that the reasons meet the exceptional permission for videolink, which, in fact, the Rule suggests is an exceptional way of hearing testimony, I want to leave it in the Chamber's hands. I wanted to make sure the Chamber knew that we had other information. And additionally, if the Chamber will permit me either later or this afternoon to make a motion about a Prosecution representative to be present in the hearing as well, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an interpretation that you're asking a representative of the Prosecution to be present at the hearing, but where?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are unable -- normally we would send --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, the hearing is here. The Prosecutor is here, Mr. Simic is here, the Judges are here, and we have a video-conference. What do you mean? You mean that a representative of the Prosecution should be present at the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Frequently when videolink takes place in other cases, a member of the Prosecution staff will be present in the event something is needed to be taken in the way of documents or some assistance to the proceeding. For example, if we want to cross-examine or transmit documents, we will have a person present. It could be a junior legal officer. My request would be, and I'm not asking the Chamber at this minute to decide but think about it under Rule 89, an investigator is normally permitted to be in the -- a lead investigator present in the courtroom with consent of the Chamber, and I would be asking, if there is no objection, for one of our investigators to be allowed, as needed, to be physically present at the hearing, but again I'm not -- this is the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "hearing." Do you mean hearing here or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- do you mean hearing in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Physically in Banja Luka. Physically in Banja Luka. And it cannot be done without the consent of the Chamber that that -- again, I didn't want -- as long as we're discussing it, if the Chamber has no objection to my raising it now so that all issues concerning the technical side of things would be handled, but if the Chamber on Mr. Simic's point, if the Chamber is satisfied otherwise, then we would -- we leave it in the Chamber's hands and we will try our best to get the cross-examination done expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As you know, there's always a representative of the Registry, and that provides the necessary assurances. Otherwise, we would have to have a representative of the Defence counsel and then maybe the Judges will say, "Why not a judge too?" and then in the end the whole thing changes anyway, the Chamber will decide about this. Mr. Jovan Simic, do you have anything to add at all? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We just were trying to economise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Ms. Susan Somers. We have to economise and bear that in mind, economy. So we're having a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am deeply convinced that we'll be much more efficacious by 3.00 p.m. from now on. We have two witnesses for today and two witnesses for tomorrow. And having said that, the Defence calls its eighth witness, with your indulgence, Mr. President, if we may, and he is Mr. Miroslav Dzebric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Usher. Would you have the witness shown in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzebric. Can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please approach the microphone, try and get comfortable, and you will start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. Deretic who is the gentleman standing to your left. Mr. Deretic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzebric, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, would you give us your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Dzebric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, 1968.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: I reside in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any children?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb and Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: I am a machine technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Since before the war because he played the guitar, and he was a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war broke out in the Prijedor municipality, did you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Usually in the coffee bars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, were you -- did you spend any time with him in his company?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war came to the Prijedor municipality, did you have occasion at all to go to his house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: No, just once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: That was a month after I was wounded and a month after my birthday, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in my arms, my legs, my chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you wounded as a member of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: In Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific and tell us the date you were with Zoran at his home?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: As I was born on the 20 -- as I was wounded on the 23rd, it was the 24th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month and year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: The 24th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that particular day, when did you meet Zoran?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: I met Zoran at around noon in the Bentley coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what he was wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a camouflage uniform and a red beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember whether on that occasion he had a bandage of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a bandage on his left hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember on that 24th what time of day it was when you met Zoran Zigic in the Bentley coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: At about 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody else with you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes, a friend of mine. He's a Muslim. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may we move into private session for a few moments, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were in that company, were there any -- anybody else apart from the three of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: No, only the three of us on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: We sat around drinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Well, it was dusk, 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Zoran Zigic suggested we have a barbecue at his place, so we went off to his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the Bentley coffee bar located in town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: The Bentley coffee bar is by the big bypass, overpass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? How far is the Zigic house away from that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Well, it took us about 15 minutes by car, 10 to 15 minutes by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop over anywhere, stop off?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Nascar restaurant to buy some meat for the barbecue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to the Zigic yard, did you find anybody there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
utterances.text: His neighbours were there, his father and mother and some other neighbours. Nikica Janjic was there. There were a number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any relations of the friend you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DZEBRIC
